text: Laughing hard, the fool spreads one hand over his face and peers out between the fingers. In his other hand he holds a pair of spectacles he is not using. Most Fool cards show a figure about to step off a cliff while looking at the sky; this one stays where he is. Kierkegaard called anxiety the dizziness of freedom, the vertigo of simply having possibilities, and set it apart from fear, which has an object, like rent. Both can arrive together, and the fear is not foolish. Taking in every option at once is what makes the head spin. A gap between two fingers is narrower, and one possibility at a time fits through it.
prompt: Name one option you have, however small, without deciding anything about it.

text: Between two fingers, a man in a tall black hat holds up a small ball, high enough for everyone to watch. That is the whole craft of the trick: the raised hand decides where the eyes go. The tarot Magician stands for mastery, tools laid out and put to use; this deck looks at the performance around the tools. A confident delivery directs attention, and it can be entirely sincere. What it cannot do is establish what is known. The same goes for anyone presenting, you included. Clarity looks plainer: what was checked, what was assumed, and a plain line between the two.

Still water, a small boat, and a figure in white standing in it, facing a rocky island. At the island's center tall cypresses grow close together, and whatever lies between them cannot be seen from the water. The High Priestess traditionally sits before a veil, keeping what is not yet known. Some questions at work are like that grove: what will be decided, what was said in a meeting you were not in. Rowing around the island again does not part the trees. A thought can be closed for today without being answered, and closing it is not agreeing that it should stay hidden. Whatever can be answered today is usually smaller, and nearer.
prompt: A question with nothing new to tell you today can wait behind the trees.

text: Her horned headdress spreads twice as wide as her head. Matsys dressed her in a fashion decades out of date, and the picture has long been read as mockery; this deck leaves the joke out. What remains is a figure wearing more than she can comfortably carry. The Empress is the card of abundance: things growing, ideas arriving. Abundance turns into a list, and an idea you raise can come back as a task with your name on it. Byung-Chul Han describes people driving themselves harder because the work feels freely chosen. When the demand comes from outside, the limit is not something to fix by trying harder. Ideas can keep arriving; the week does not stretch to hold them.

Authority does not always arrive with a face. “We have decided”, “the team feels”, “leadership wants”: a decision can reach you as a chorus. Fuseli painted three faces in a row under one pale cloak, arms stretched out to point, overlapping so closely that it is hard to say whose hand is whose. He took the three from Macbeth, but the picture works without the play: several people, one gesture, no single owner. The Emperor usually means one ruler and a visible structure. A claim made in chorus may be accurate. It can also be one view in a plural voice. Who decided, and on what basis, is what the chorus leaves out.

Every page of the book shows donkeys, rank after rank, and the donkey reading it studies them closely. Goya's plate is a lineage offered as proof of standing. The Hierophant keeps tradition, and tradition can carry real knowledge. It can also be cited as its own reason. Roland Barthes called this tautology: answering why with because that is how it is, and closing the question there. Out loud it sounds like “that is how we do it here.” When you are told you fell short, the expectation you missed should be one somebody can point to. Taking responsibility for a real lapse is easier when the rule has a text, and not only a history.
prompt: Is there a written rule behind the expectation you were measured against? Looking it up privately is enough.

text: Tweedledum and Tweedledee look exactly alike, and in Tenniel's drawing they are doing opposite things: one stamps and clutches his head, the other has crawled under an umbrella with only his feet showing. Alice stands beside them. Two yeses given on different days can be twins like that: same word, same goodwill. Then they land in the same week, and one is loud while the other stays hidden until it is late. Where most Lovers cards ask which path to take, the choice here is narrower: which commitment gets the hours. Choosing one leaves the other standing. What changes is that someone says plainly what it will now get, and when.
prompt: Of two things you said yes to, which is louder right now, and which matters more to you?

text: A small boy holding a commander's baton sits calmly on a horse rearing high on its hind legs. The rearing looks wild, but in royal portraits of the time it showed a trained movement: the horse rises in place, on command, and holds there. The usual Chariot shows a driver keeping two opposing forces in line. Many work processes look like that horse, full of motion and height, all of it rising in place. Somewhere beneath them, a person decided where the effort goes, and when. That decision is often older and smaller than the process built on it. Finding it, and whose it was, says more than the motion does.

Whistler called it Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, though most people know it by its sitter, his mother. She sits in profile, back straight, hands folded over a handkerchief, looking ahead. Nothing in the pose pushes. The traditional Strength card shows a woman closing a lion's jaws with her bare hands; there is no lion here. A precise question at work can have the same shape as this posture: upright, asking only what it asks. Calm is not a condition for it, and a question asked in a shaking voice is just as precise. How it is received depends partly on power, which is outside your control. A question about the criterion remains a question about the work.
prompt: If you had one precise question about your work, what would it be? Writing it down is enough for now.

text: Replies thin out, a thread goes silent, and nobody says why. Quiet like that was not chosen. Dürer's Jerome chose his: he writes at his desk, head bent, entirely absorbed, while a lion and a small dog lie asleep on the floor in front of him. The Hermit withdraws in order to see clearly. From outside, the two kinds of stillness look alike. Imposed quiet tends to fill up with explanations. Jerome's attention to the page still helps there. What happened can be written down plainly, with dates if you have them, and the motive left blank until something actually supplies one.

Some meetings end by scheduling the next one, and the week goes round. Tenniel's Mad Tea-Party has the same shape. The Hatter explains that Time stopped for him after a quarrel, so it is always six o'clock, always tea-time, and there is never a moment to wash the cups; they move round the table to clean ones instead. The Dormouse sleeps through it. The Wheel of Fortune turns by luck, with nobody steering; a meeting wheel is one people built. The hours spent going round are real hours, taken from work that could move. The clock kept moving, even when the decision didn't.

Daumier's advocate leans far over the bar, mouth open, the whole weight of his argument in his shoulders. The picture is all speech; the case itself is nowhere in it. Justice holds a scale, and a scale needs something named on each side. Kafka's Josef K., arrested one morning without being told the charge, comes to think he must write an account of his entire life for the court. When criticism arrives with no stated example or standard, the pull is to answer it the same way, at length and in every direction. A specific question can be fair, and its answer uncomfortable. One question can still be answered. A whole life cannot.
prompt: Notice what single question, if any, has actually been put to you.

text: A draft waits for sign-off; a project waits on a decision that sits on someone else's desk. From underneath, the stalled thing can look like your problem, and the waiting like your delay. Tenniel's Father William stands on his head, feet in the air, while a young man with a stick looks on, one palm open, waiting for it to make sense. The Hanged One hangs upside down too, in most readings by choice, seeing the world from a reversed angle. Work is often suspended by someone other than the person doing it. Naming the decision it hangs on, and who holds it, puts the suspension back where it belongs.

An old man bent over a crutch walks into a dark doorway. On the stone above it a young figure sits up, looking skyward. Blake designed the two together for a poem about the grave, and the engraving keeps them on one block of stone. Tarot's Death card means an ending rather than a literal death, and this deck does not claim that every ending leads somewhere better. Tasks reach a doorway too: a requirement superseded, a report nobody opens any more. Keeping one alive takes effort that its lost purpose no longer repays. Letting it go through is reasonable. So is noticing, on the way, what it took to build.
prompt: Is there a task you keep tending that has already been superseded? You can name it without dropping it yet.

text: Helmet still on, Mars has sat down. His chin rests on his hand, a staff hangs loosely from the other, and in the full painting his shield and armour lie on the floor at his feet. Velázquez gave the god of war a heavy, thoughtful face. The Temperance card shows an angel pouring between two cups, a measured flow rather than a flood. Capacity has a measure too. More requests do not make more hours; they divide the same ones thinner, and strength does not change that arithmetic. Saying how much fits into a week is a description of the hours. That is easier to say once the measure is visible: what is in hand, and what is being asked.

The moneylender weighs coins on a small balance with complete care. Beside him his wife turns a page of an illuminated prayer book, but her eyes have moved to the coins. The painting is often read as a contrast between worldly and spiritual devotion. Something plainer is visible too: money pulls attention, even from someone in the middle of something else. The Devil card traditionally shows chains loose enough to lift off, as if leaving were simple. This deck does not assume that. Income is a real need, and so is the fear of losing it. The picture also shows her hand, still on the page. Attention can be pulled without judgment going with it.
prompt: Name one thing you care about that this job does not touch.

text: Bruegel's tower is unfinished. The lower tiers are pale and complete; higher up, raw red brick shows where building is still going on, wrapped around a hill of bare rock. In Genesis the work stops when the builders' language is confused and they can no longer understand one another. The tarot Tower is struck by lightning and falls, and this deck does not celebrate collapse. Bruegel shows a more ordinary version: a structure halted midway because the terms changed under the people building it. When acceptance criteria move after the work is done, the gap was made by the change. Setting the old criteria next to the new ones keeps the record straight, whatever happens next.

Redon drew an eye the size of a balloon, rising into a pale sky. Its iris is turned upward, toward the infinity of the title, and a small head hangs beneath it where the basket would be. In the Major Arcana the Star follows the Tower: a light to steer by after upheaval. This card trades the star for an eye, and the feeling it speaks to is being watched. Scrutiny is real, it can have consequences, and noticing it is reasonable. Still, being looked at and being found wanting are separate facts. Only the second needs a finding: something specific, said by someone, about the work. Attention alone does not say what it has found.

Both hands pressed to its head, mouth open in an oval, Munch's figure has become shorthand for fear. Munch wrote that he felt a scream passing through nature, so the figure may be shutting a sound out as much as making one. Under the tarot Moon, shapes look larger than they are; this deck does not assume the fear is illusion. Rollo May separated normal anxiety, proportionate to a real threat, from anxiety out of proportion to it, and did not treat the first as something to cure. Fear about work can be fully proportionate. Checking the facts asks no one to feel less; it sets the exact words said beside the outcome the fear already pictures.
prompt: None of that checking has to happen tonight.

text: An owl strums a small guitar, and a cat sits with one paw on a jar marked HONEY, the two of them in a very small boat. In Lear's poem they also packed plenty of money, wrapped up in a five-pound note, and went to sea. Nothing in the picture is work. The Sun card usually shows full daylight, everything going well at once. This deck swaps it for something smaller. After a hard stretch at work, every day can start to feel like a test, graded on what it produced. Some days hold very little: a song, something sweet, a slow crossing. A day like that hasn't failed at anything. It was an ordinary day, and ordinary has its own kind of daylight.

Five heads crowd the top of the tower on this elephant's back, helmets and hoods close enough to talk without raising their voices. Bestiaries told of elephants carrying soldiers into war in towers like this one. The traditional Judgement card is a summons, an angel's trumpet calling the dead to rise. This deck turns to a different kind of verdict: the one that forms among people who share a vantage point. Talk about a colleague can work like that tower. It can pass on something true, or a story nobody checked, and repeated at close quarters it starts to sound like a view. What you have seen of someone yourself is slower evidence, and it is yours.

When Bosch's triptych is closed, its two outer wings show a world in grey: a clear sphere with a flat disc of land inside, clouds overhead, no people yet. It is usually read as the world early in its making. Open the shutters and the crowded garden appears. Closing them again does not finish the world; it shows that a whole can be shut while it is still being made. The World card traditionally means completion, which work rarely offers. A day can stop anyway, with a plain account of what is done and what is still open. Then the panels can close, and the rest of your life, the part no task list covers, carries on.

In Redon's Crying Spider, drawn in 1881, a large face sits where its body should be, a tear on one cheek, carried on long thin legs. Feelings at work often arrive like that, in the middle of things: hurt at a remark made in passing, dread when your name comes up in a meeting. The Ace of Cups shows a single cup running over, a feeling arriving whole before anything is done with it. Letting it be there is one act. Replying is another, even if it follows only seconds later. The tear stays on the face. Where the legs go is decided separately.
prompt: Before your next reply, name the feeling to yourself in one word. The reply can come after.

text: Two people stand side by side, his right hand raised, her hand resting in his left, and art historians have long argued over what exactly the scene records. Even a picture this precise leaves the terms open. The Two of Cups is a pledge between two people. Pledges at work are usually smaller and more practical: who owns a task, what done means, by when. Spoken agreements like that feel solid in the moment and drift afterwards, often without anyone lying, because each person remembers the version that fit their week. Writing it down does not change who has more power. It gives both people the same version to point to.

Donkey, dog, cat and rooster stand one on top of another, four animals making one tall shape. In the Grimm tale each had an owner who no longer wanted it, and stacked at a window they frightened a band of robbers out of their house. The Three of Cups traditionally celebrates friendship and shared good fortune. Workplaces have that, and also its harder relative: the alliance, which can form for good reasons and still come with a side to take. From outside a stack, staying out can feel like being shut out, and sometimes it does cost something. Courtesy toward each member and a place in the stack are different commitments. The second can be declined quietly, without a speech.

Two of Goya's hobgoblins stand together in monks' habits, grinning, each with a cup already in hand. The taller one has raised his free hand mid-gesture; the hooded one keeps his cup close. In the usual Four of Cups someone ignores a fourth cup held out to them, and the old reading calls that apathy or ingratitude. This card drops that reading. A hand already holding something cannot take more without setting something down. At work the full hand is often invisible: three commitments running, each with its share of the week, none of them on the list being discussed. Declining a fourth can be arithmetic rather than reluctance. Counting what you already hold makes the arithmetic visible.

Nothing in Haeckel's spider weeps, whatever the card's title says. Drawn from above for a book of natural forms, it is all exactness: striped legs spread, a pale pattern on its back, every part where it is. The Five of Cups traditionally shows someone grieving three spilled cups while two still stand, and the usual advice is to count the two. Simone Weil warned against imaginary consolation, comfort invented to avoid looking at a loss. A naturalist's eye offers a different kind of help: it records what is there and leaves nothing out. Facing an outcome that way means listing what went and what stayed, at their real size, and letting neither erase the other.

A young man leans over a stone ledge, intent on a thin straw, while a small child watches from just below. In Chardin's time, soap bubbles were a familiar image for things that do not last. The Six of Cups looks back fondly, to childhood and old kindnesses. The warm thing that comes back is often a promise: the promotion next cycle, the role that will open once things settle, the workload that eases next quarter. Hearing it again can feel like being looked after. A promise can be sincere every time and still not arrive. Fresh attention compares this version with the last: what was said then, what happened, what is said now.

Look at the creature long enough and it still will not settle: a cracked, speckled body like a clay pot, a frog's legs, a dark pointed head pushing out of an opening at one end. Bosch filled his pictures with hybrids like this, and commentators have never agreed on what they mean. The Seven of Cups is a row of visions, each tempting, none certain. An instruction can end up the same way after enough retellings: part of what was said in the meeting, part of the follow-up email, part of a comment made in passing. When the thing itself keeps changing shape, asking what it is today is an accurate response, and it needs no apology attached.
prompt: Could you write the current instruction in one sentence? Notice where the sentence runs out.

text: The man stands with his back to us, a walking stick in his hand; the famous view of mountains and fog has been cut away. What is left is the posture of someone who has stepped back far enough to see. The Eight of Cups traditionally shows a figure walking away from what no longer holds them; here the departure is smaller: out of one exchange, not a job. Karl Jaspers held that real communication needs both people open to each other. Rank and pressure often rule that out, whatever anyone intends. When a conversation keeps circling, stepping back is not abandoning it. You stop adding turns to the loop and look at its shape.
prompt: Picture one professional way to pause an exchange that keeps circling. You do not have to use it.

text: Nobody in this portrait is laughing. The title came later; Hals painted a half-smile under an upturned moustache, a hand on the hip, a sleeve embroidered in fine detail. The Nine of Cups puts contentment on display, a satisfied man before his row of cups. Arlie Hochschild described two ways of meeting a job's demand for feeling. In surface acting you shape the expression and keep your own feeling underneath. In deep acting you work on the feeling itself until it matches. The first takes effort, and it leaves something private behind the face. Professional work asks for the expression and the deliverable. A professional face is sometimes what gets you through. It doesn't have to be the whole truth about how you feel.

Six men in black look up from a table as though someone has just come in. Their office was judging the quality of dyed cloth, and Rembrandt painted them mid-glance, nearly every face turned toward the viewer. It is easy to feel assessed by a group like this. Look again and the group comes apart: one is half out of his chair, one keeps a hand on the open book, one has no hat and stands behind the others. The Ten of Cups traditionally shows a contented household; this card turns to the crowd that seems to hold a single opinion. A remark comes from one person. A group's silence is several separate silences, and each could mean something different.

Paws flung up, mouth wide open, cape flying: Doré's Puss in Boots cries out with his whole body. In the story he is a messenger, carrying gifts and messages to the king on his master's behalf. A feeling at work can arrive at that volume. Anxiety before a review, embarrassment after a mistake, irritation in a meeting: each carries a message about what matters to you and what seems at risk. The Page of Cups brings a message from the heart, often in an unexpected form. How loud a feeling is tells you how much is at stake. It does not tell you how good you are at your job, and it was never measuring that.

Cropped like this, the picture shows a woman in pink in the middle of a swing, one foot kicked high, the ropes taut. Fragonard's full canvas holds more: a man working the swing's ropes from the shadows, another lying in the bushes below, watching. Take them away and the story changes, though every pink brushstroke is still his. Rumors work this way. A real detail, cut from its surroundings, arrives charming and complete. The Knight of Cups rides in with an invitation, and a good rumor is one: to be on the inside, to share a judgment about someone who is not there to answer. Passing it on adds your name to a version you have not checked.

Many workplaces run partly on one person: the colleague who notices who is struggling, who absorbs tension so a meeting can go on. That care is real work, and it rarely appears in a job description. Vermeer's girl has turned to look over her shoulder, lips slightly parted, all her attention on whoever is standing there. Yet the painting is about her. The light falls on her face, on the pearl, on the folds of the turban. The Queen of Cups is the one people bring their troubles to. Care that leaves out the person giving it turns into one more part of the workload. Whoever turns toward others also deserves to be turned toward.
prompt: Some of today's care can go to you.

text: Raphael painted his friend Baldassare Castiglione with his hands clasped, his clothes in muted grey and black, his blue eyes level with ours. Nothing in the face hurries. The King of Cups is the master of feeling, enthroned calmly on a rough sea. Composure like this is easy to admire and easy to misread. A steady face in a tense meeting is no proof that the feelings have gone; often they are right there, unsettled, while the sentence gets chosen anyway. This card asks for the measured sentence. Emptying yourself first was never part of the request. The steadiness and the unrest can share the same moment.
prompt: Is there one measured sentence that would be true, with the feeling still beside it? It can stay unsaid.

text: Leonardo drew this man twice over in the same ink: arms level and arms raised, feet together and feet apart. Short ruled marks cross the body where he measured it. Two positions share one figure and nothing blurs, because each was drawn whole. Confusion at work often comes from two versions stacked on top of each other with no line between them: last month's scope and this month's, the plan as announced and the plan as run. The Ace of Pentacles is a beginning you can hold in your hand. An outline is that kind of beginning. It cannot decide which version wins, but it spares you from guessing where one ends and the other starts.

Vermeer's woman holds a balance so fine it barely shows, and waits for it to settle. Examined closely, its pans are empty. The Two of Pentacles traditionally shows someone juggling two loads; this card slows the juggling down to the moment of weighing. Some of what you are asked to balance is yours to weigh. Some of it is a decision that belongs to someone else and has not been made, and no care on your side can fill that pan. Guessing the missing answer, then carrying the guess as if it were settled, becomes a second load, and an invisible one. An unanswered question stays unanswered, however carefully it is weighed.
prompt: Which of the loads you are carrying is actually yours to weigh?

text: A backlog can refill as fast as you clear it. Courbet's stonebreakers work beside a road: one raises a hammer, the other hauls a basket of what is already broken, and there is always more stone. The Three of Pentacles celebrates shared craft, a building finished and admired; this is the other end of the trade. Hannah Arendt distinguished labor, consumed almost as fast as it is produced, from work, which leaves something that lasts. A backlog is labor in her sense. Its endlessness comes from how the work is set up, not from your speed or your worth. A pile like that calls for a decision, often someone else's, about what gets dropped. Effort alone cannot settle that.

Filled through the hole in its head and tipped forward to pour, this bronze lion was made to wash hands at table or altar. Whatever it was asked to pour had to go in first. The Four of Pentacles is the card of holding tight, and work often stalls at that grip: a login, a budget line, the one file only one person can open. A lock can be policy, caution or plain neglect, and from outside you rarely know which. Either way, the work is waiting on access, not on effort. Saying which access the work is waiting on describes the work; it accuses no one.
prompt: Is any of your work waiting on a key you do not hold?

text: Some shortages get absorbed quietly: too few people, a tool that never arrived, hours that do not add up. On a hard wooden bench in Daumier's third-class carriage sit three people: a young woman nursing a baby, an older woman with both hands on a basket, a boy asleep against her side. Nobody complains, and nobody has put anything down. The Five of Pentacles is hardship endured out in the cold; this card moves it indoors. Absorbed long enough, a gap stops looking like a gap and starts to look like the amount you are supposed to carry. Naming what is missing, without having to solve it, puts it back where it can be seen.
prompt: What has been missing from your work that you have quietly been covering?

text: One more check, one more revision, one more proof: some requests never reach an end. Gillray drew three diners around a single bowl of gold coins, each lifting a spoon to the mouth, each with a pouch hanging at the throat, two of them swollen as large as a head. He was mocking real people and their appetite for public money; this card leaves the mockery and keeps the bowl. The Six of Pentacles is about exchange across a gap in power: who gives, who receives, on what terms. Terms include an end. A demand that can always ask for more has stopped working like an exchange and started working like appetite. A definition of finished gives your effort somewhere to arrive.
prompt: What would “finished” look like for the task that keeps coming back?

text: Racknitz drew the chess machine as he believed it worked, walls cut away. On top sits the robed player audiences saw. Inside the cabinet a man in a red coat bends over a small board by candlelight, making the moves himself. New systems are often introduced as if they run on their own. Someone is usually inside: learning the new steps and filling gaps by hand. That person needs what the man in the cabinet had, a view of the board and light to see it. The Seven of Pentacles is a pause to look over what the work has grown. After a change, that pause includes asking where the new way is written down, and why.

In this copy after Chardin, a monkey in a scholar's robe holds a magnifying glass to a coin, books open beside him. Chardin's original mocked collectors; only the glass is kept here. The Eight of Pentacles is patient craft. Rollo May distinguished being aware of yourself as the one doing something from watching yourself as an object others will judge. Work that passes through many reviewers pulls toward the coin's side of the glass: attention drifts from the task to the people waiting to inspect it, each with a different idea of good. Inspection is a different act from ownership. Until someone is named who can call the work finished, no single opinion can close it.
prompt: If one person had to call this work finished, who would it be? “I don’t know” is an answer too.

text: The traditional Nine of Pentacles shows a woman alone in her garden, a hooded bird on her glove, at ease among things she has earned. Bruegel's monkeys sit at the other end: chained to one ring, one facing out, one curled with its head down. The chain fixes where they sit. It says nothing about what they can do. Constant availability is that kind of tether: it records that you are reachable, nothing about your skill. What you know how to do is still there at the end of the day, on a weekend, during a slow reply. Where a job truly requires you to be reachable, that is a term of the job, and terms have edges.
prompt: Pick one point today after which this piece of work can wait.

text: Las Meninas is crowded with roles: the painter with his brush raised, the young princess at the center, a maid of honor kneeling at her side, a chaperone half in shadow, a large dog lying in front. Every person has a set place in the court's order. The Ten of Pentacles is the card of inheritance and established wealth, an order that outlasts the people inside it. Processes are inherited the same way. Steps get added for reasons that later leave, and the steps stay. Asking for the shortest route to done is a question about the map, which anyone working inside it is entitled to ask. It leaves everyone in the picture standing where they are.

Apart from a bristling grey beard, this figure is built of books: an open volume fanned out for hair, bound ones stacked into a chest and arms. He is made of what is already on the shelf. An agenda that never finishes invites the opposite habit: preparing for every requirement that might arrive, until nothing is learned because everything is still being anticipated. The Page of Pentacles is a student, careful and new, learning by handling the material itself. What you already know is that material. A question you still need answered is a different kind of thing, worth writing down on its own, so the known part can be worked on today.

Dürer never saw this rhinoceros. In 1515 he worked from a written description and a sketch sent from Lisbon, and he rendered every plate, rivet and scale with patient care, adding a small twisted horn on the shoulder that no real rhinoceros has. The Knight of Pentacles is traditionally the slow, thorough worker, and thoroughness is a real virtue. Its limit shows here. More detail could not supply what the description left out; that needed the animal, or someone who had seen it. Due diligence has the same limit. Past a certain point another review only adds plating, when what the work is missing is a decision with someone's name on it.
prompt: Which open item here needs a decision rather than one more check?

text: Georg Gisze, a German merchant working in London, holds an opened letter; beside him, carnations stand in a glass vase. Outside this crop, Holbein filled the office with the tools of keeping order: more letters, seals, scales, pens. The Queen of Pentacles is the one who tends, the practical keeper of what everyone else relies on. Gathering scattered requests into one list is that kind of work. It makes everyone else's work easier and rarely gets counted as work itself. A written list of what was agreed has a second use as well: it holds the agreement somewhere outside anyone's memory, including yours.
prompt: If you wrote down only what has actually been agreed, how long would the list be?

text: Böcklin painted himself at work, brush and palette in hand, with a skeleton leaning in behind his ear. In the full painting it plays a one-string fiddle. His brush has stopped, and he seems to be listening. For Böcklin the tune was mortality; this card borrows only where it sits, close and in the background. A warning feeling plays like that, and it registers something true, often the distance between you and whoever has more power. Documented risk is information of another kind: a date, a written decision, a change in terms. The two often arrive together. The King of Pentacles is material steadiness, and here it looks like two columns, each weighed for what it is.

Waterhouse's Thisbe leans in with one hand raised to her ear, listening for every word. In Ovid's story she and Pyramus could talk only through a crack in a wall, in the faintest whisper. Words at work cross walls of their own. A sentence gets forwarded, summarized or quoted somewhere else, without its tone. That is ordinary. In a heated moment the pull is toward the sentence anger offers, which is rarely the one you would want repeated. The Ace of Swords is a single clean edge: one plain sentence. Plainness can feel like giving ground. What it keeps is a record of your own words you can stand behind, wherever they travel.
prompt: If a reply is waiting, which sentence in it would you be comfortable hearing repeated?

text: Alice stands between the Lion and the Unicorn, holding a large dish of cake. In Carroll's story she has been trying to cut it, and the slices keep joining up again, until the Unicorn explains that looking-glass cake is handed round first and cut afterwards. Nobody mentioned that rule until she had already failed at the old one. The Two of Swords shows a figure caught between two pressures, unable to move cleanly toward either. When a requirement shifts and different people hold different versions, guessing which one is current puts the whole risk of being wrong on you. Asking which version applies is a plain factual question. Whoever owns the rule owns the answer, too.

Tenniel's three gardeners are playing cards with heads and hands, a paint pot at their feet. In Carroll's chapter they planted a white rose tree by mistake and are painting its roses red before the Queen's procession arrives, since she answers mistakes with “Off with their heads!” The mistake concerned a tree; the penalty concerned the gardeners. The Three of Swords is the card of the wound that words make, and nothing here calls that wound small. Pointed criticism can land like the Queen's sentence, as if it were about the whole person. Feedback usually points at a tree: one piece of work, which can be answered with work. The person who planted it is a separate matter.
prompt: If a comment is still stinging, what piece of work was it actually about, if any?

text: In Rousseau's painting a lion stands over a sleeping figure in a striped robe, a mandolin and a water jug beside her. The lion stands over her, and the picture does not say what it will do. The Four of Swords is traditionally a card of rest, a figure lying still with the swords set aside. Feeling small in front of someone with more power gets the proportions right. As a count of options it is poor, because it reports only the large ones: fight, or give in. Smaller ones usually remain: a pause, a request for details, time to read before answering. None of them changes the size of the lion.
prompt: Waiting counts as one of the options.

text: Bruegel's Carnival rides astride a barrel, a roasting spit for a lance and a pot hanging below him, while a man in a fool's cap follows with a jug. His opponent, outside the crop, is Lent: thin, armed with a baker's peel and two fish. Their fight came round every year, and the calendar always settled it: Lent comes after Carnival. The Five of Swords is the card of a contest that costs more than it gains. Some contests at work look like that, settled somewhere else before anyone starts, and staying quiet can be the sensible choice. Silence still has a price: it leaves you guessing at what is expected. Asking for those expectations in writing is a different move from a fight. It asks for no victory, only for terms you can see.
prompt: Is there one expectation you are guessing at that you would rather see in writing?

text: Hokusai's ghost grips the edge of a mosquito net with bony fingers and peers over it. A finished conversation can come back like that: late, uninvited, leaning over the edge of sleep. Each pass brings a sharper line, a better reply, another reading of a pause. Replaying is what a mind does after a hard exchange, and it shows what mattered. What it cannot do is change what was said. The Six of Swords is a passage across water, one shore left behind for another. Here the shore is a conversation that has ended. Its facts are fixed, and they will keep until working hours, which is where anything still to be done with them belongs.

Seated upright, Goya's donkey poses for a portrait while a monkey works at the easel. The plate was satire; this card borrows only the pose. A portrait can record a pose exactly and say nothing about what the sitter knows. Titles, a confident tone and long experience work like that pose: reasons to listen, not evidence. Authority does not make a conclusion wrong, either. The Seven of Swords is the card of things kept out of sight; here the hidden part is what a conclusion rests on. Wanting to see that accuses no one. A specific answer shows its basis; a credential only frames it.

Each man in Bruegel's line holds a staff or a shoulder of the man ahead, most of their faces turned upward. Toward the front, one is already falling. The painting follows a saying from the Gospels: if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the ditch. The Eight of Swords traditionally shows a figure bound and blindfolded; here the binding is the line itself. In a chain of approvals, each nod makes the next one easier. Going along can be the safer choice, and only you can weigh that. Where there is room to speak, saying you see it differently can be entirely courteous, and it leaves open the chance that you are the one who has it wrong.
prompt: Is there something you have nodded along to that you see differently? Noticing it is enough for now.

text: Late at night a worry grows by addition: one more scenario, one more reply you should have sent. Goya's figure has put his head down on his arms, and behind him the creatures gather, an owl, a large cat watching steadily. The plate's title says the sleep of reason produces monsters, and the Spanish word sueño means both sleep and dream, so it reads either way. The Nine of Swords is the card of the night that will not end. Writing down one fact gives the worry something fixed to stand beside. Writing more tends to feed it. One line is enough, and the rest can wait for daylight.

Uccello's dragon stands on two legs, wings spread and marked with round spots like eyes, tail curled behind it. It takes up half the picture. Fear does that: whatever it is about fills the view, and it often knows something real about the danger. The Ten of Swords traditionally marks the lowest point, a painful end. This card borrows the dragon and leaves that forecast out. The knight's lance does not try to meet the whole dragon; it meets one point, the open mouth. The fear can stay in the picture. Coming back to the next fact is a narrower move: one point, then the one after it.
prompt: Under the fear right now, what is the next small fact or task in front of you?

text: Tenniel's White Rabbit checks his pocket watch, umbrella tucked under one arm, already in a hurry. In the first chapter, Alice has only a rabbit saying “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!”, and she follows him down the hole “never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.” The Page of Swords is a messenger, carrying news before anyone knows what it means. A rumor arrives the same way, with urgency attached, and the urgency belongs to whoever is carrying it. The content is often a fragment: no source, no date, no decision. Asking where it came from keeps a fragment a fragment, instead of following it down into a verdict.
prompt: Before passing on anything urgent, notice whose urgency it is.

text: Every bone in Van der Gucht's skeleton is drawn with care, down to the small joints of the clasped hands. It is an anatomy plate, meant to be accurate. The pose is another matter. No skeleton kneels to pray; someone chose that pose. A vivid scenario gets assembled like that pose. Its parts are often real, a tone, a date, a phrase from a meeting, and the mind arranges them into a scene that has not happened. The Knight of Swords charges ahead at full speed, and so does a mind building that scene. The fear driving it knows what you would hate to lose. Accurate parts still do not confirm the arrangement.
prompt: You don't have to finish the scene to put it down.

text: The Queen of Hearts points with her whole arm, and Alice stands in front of her, upright and much smaller. In the book, Alice's first answer to her is short and polite: “My name is Alice, so please your Majesty.” The Queen of Swords is the card of a clear, unpadded statement. Under pressure the pull is to add reasons until a limit sounds deserved. Manuel J. Smith, writing about assertiveness, argued that people do not owe a justification for every choice they make. Some reasons are owed; the extra ones, offered out of fear, are another matter. Each one hands the listener something more to dispute. A brief, specific limit can still be courteous.
prompt: Is there one sentence your limit could do without?

text: Crowned, beaked and scaled, with a row of short legs and a tail that curls into a hook, the basilisk in Aldrovandi's book was drawn from reports, not from life. Legend gave it a gaze that killed whoever met it, so nobody could study it directly. Blame without a stated standard can work similarly: felt, repeated, hard to look at closely. The King of Swords stands for judgment by clear principles, authority that shows its reasons. A verdict from someone above you carries weight whatever its quality. A criterion you can see is a different thing: something to aim at and check work against. Requesting one accepts the authority and asks only that the judgment become visible.

God's arm stretches toward the left edge of this crop, and Adam is not in the picture at all. What remains is the reach, before anything has been touched. The Ace of Wands is that moment: a first spark of interest. Interest is quickly converted into commitment. Saying an idea sounds exciting can be heard as volunteering, and the hours that follow can get counted as enthusiasm rather than work. Sarah Jaffe has written about how love for a job is used to justify long hours and thin pay. The interest is still yours, and it can stay a reach for a while, until you know what taking hold would cost.
prompt: What would this idea need from you before you could say yes to it?

text: The Two of Wands traditionally shows a figure holding a small globe, weighing where to go next. Holbein's two ambassadors once stood on either side of a shelf crowded with globes and instruments for measuring the world. This crop takes all of it away and leaves white space between the two men. Planning needs that kind of space. When every request arrives marked urgent, the space fills, and everything looks equally on fire. The loudness of an alarm tells you how it was sent; it says little about what depends on the answer. Some alarms really are urgent. Telling which ones usually comes down to a quieter question: what happens if this waits a day?

Friedrich painted these two men looking at the moon. The crop takes the moon away and keeps the looking: two backs, two caps, one man's hand resting on the other's shoulder. The Three of Wands shows a figure on high ground, watching ships set out and waiting for what comes back. At work, the thing on the horizon is often a change on its way: a reorganization, a new system, a season of deadlines. Seeing it from a distance is not the same as being under it. The hand on the shoulder changes nothing about what is coming. It changes what it is like to stand there and watch. Not everyone has that at work, and where someone does stand beside you, it counts for more than it looks.

Medieval bestiaries held that the salamander could live in fire. This one lies stretched along a bed of red flames, head raised, tail curled, as if the flames were a mattress. The belief was wrong, and the picture is here for its strangeness, not as advice on keeping cool. Nobody is fireproof. A deadline's heat is real, and it produces motion: rereading the same message, apologizing in advance, starting three things at once. That is what heat does to people, and from inside, motion and progress feel the same. The Four of Wands usually celebrates finished work. This card is set earlier, while the finishing still has to be arranged, and the date it is measured against was often set by someone else.
prompt: If it helps, pick the one part that has to go first. The rest can wait its turn.

text: Arcimboldo built this emperor's face from a whole year's produce: wheat and grapes in the hair, a pear for a nose, cherries at the mouth, a gourd for a chest, flowers crowding the shoulders. No field yields all of it at once; spring flowers and autumn grapes do not ripen in the same week. The painting celebrates an abundance no garden produces. Workloads get built like this: each request reasonable in its own season, all of them due together. The Five of Wands traditionally shows a scuffle in which everyone gets in each other's way; here the crowding is on one desk. When it all falls due at once, the shortfall belongs to the calendar, not to the person.

Delacroix painted the July Revolution of 1830 at full volume: the flag raised as high as an arm can reach, a boy running forward with a pistol in each hand. The fighting was real, and this card borrows only its volume. The Six of Wands is a public victory, carried in procession. Workplaces have their own processions: a heated thread, a reply-all that gets louder with each answer. Loudness invites more loudness, and matching it can feel like the only way to be heard. Turning your response down is a different move from giving in. A quieter answer keeps the point in view and leaves you free to raise it once the noise drops.

When a request comes back for the third or fourth time, the pressure rises; the capacity it presses on has not grown. In David's painting Leonidas sits still at the centre, a shield behind him, while the men around him reach, turn and climb. The Seven of Wands shows that kind of position: one figure on higher ground, holding a line against many staves. Albert Camus wrote that a refusal is also an affirmation: the rebel's no marks a limit beyond which something must be respected. Holding a line promises nothing about how the next round goes. The limit was true the first time, and the fourth request does not make it less true.
prompt: What, specifically, is your limit here protecting?

text: Small errors, slow replies, a moved date: each can arrive inside a reaction many times its weight. Blake painted a flea that way, as a heavy, muscled figure the size of a man, striding forward with a shallow bowl held out in one hand. The Eight of Wands is speed, things arriving through the air faster than anyone can sort them, and a reaction that big pulls you toward answering at the same pitch. Matching it is one option and rarely the only one. Sometimes the alarm fits the issue. Often the issue underneath is smaller than the body it was given, and that smaller thing is what you can actually answer, in plain words.
prompt: Leaving the size of the reaction aside, what is the issue, in one plain sentence?

text: A bandaged head belongs to the traditional Nine of Wands: a figure who has been hurt, standing guard, still watching. Van Gogh's self-portrait carries a bandage too, under a fur cap, his gaze turned slightly aside. Wariness after a hurt is a reading of real experience, and it is often accurate. It also writes forecasts: the next meeting will go badly, the next message will be bad news. A forecast feels like knowledge because it borrows the force of what already happened. It remains a guess about something that has not happened yet. Your guard can stay up while you sort which part of what you see is memory and which part is forecast.

Goya's two men walk bent under two donkeys, faces turned toward the ground. He named the plate after a Spanish saying, roughly “you who cannot, carry me on your back.” The Ten of Wands shows the same posture: someone carrying more staves than they can see past. Under that load, the ground in front is all there is, and each new thing gets picked up without being looked at. A short pause interrupts that. Asking for a moment to confirm the details is how someone under weight checks what has been handed over, whose it is, and whether it is the size it was said to be. The load is no lighter during that moment, only counted.
prompt: Is there one thing you are carrying that you picked up before checking whose it was?

text: Reynolds painted Puck as a grinning child with pointed ears, one arm flung up and a bunch of flowers in the other hand. In Shakespeare's play, Puck is the messenger sent with a flower and an instruction: find the young man in Athenian clothes. Two young men in the wood wear them, and he finds the wrong one. The instruction fit both. The Page of Wands is the student of the suit, carrying the message before learning the routine around it. Being new comes with pressure to look as if you already know, and a basic question can feel like evidence against you. Often that question is the one that tells two people apart.
prompt: What is one question about this work you have held back because it seemed too basic?

text: Doré shows the moment after the charge: Don Quixote and his horse hoisted up on a windmill sail, limbs hanging. Cervantes's knight had seen giants, and he rode at them with total conviction. The Knight of Wands has the same energy, all momentum and courage. Sometimes the threat at work is real, and it deserves a response. Sometimes what looks like a giant is a process, a policy or a misunderstanding, and charging it costs more than it wins, because the thing keeps turning on its own and takes you up with it. Checking first is not hesitation. It is finding out whether the arms you see are swinging at you or simply turning in the wind.

La Perre de Roo's English Pouter stands tall on long feathered legs, its crop blown up into a globe larger than the rest of the bird. Pouters are bred for that display. The Queen of Wands is the confident one of the suit, warm and sure of her place, and confidence at work is often expected to look like the pouter: fully inflated, every request met with yes. Keeping a display up costs effort for every hour it lasts. A confident person also knows where they end. Saying what you can offer, and what lies outside it, gives the offer a real shape. A limit stated plainly belongs to the confidence and makes the yes worth believing.
prompt: What can you offer here with confidence, and what lies outside it?

text: Ingres seats Napoleon facing straight out, the round gilded back of the throne behind his head like a halo. Laurel, ermine, velvet and gold all announce power. Both hands hold long rods of office, and nothing in the picture says what anyone is asked to do. The King of Wands is vision and command, and a large announcement can arrive like this, all splendour and no next step. Marshall Rosenberg distinguished a request, a specific action the other person is free to decline, from a demand, where refusing brings blame or punishment. From above, even a request can carry that weight. Knowing what decision is needed, and from whom, turns the announcement into something a person can answer.
prompt: If this announcement turned into one request, what would the request be?
